A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LoFT research work. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic optimization experiments and fine-tuning results for commonsense reasoning, image classification, mathematical reasoning, and language modeling.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds component ablations, efficiency measurements, CIFAR-100 comparisons, 70B-model evaluation, and code-generation experiments.

M1.justification: v2 develops v1's proposed future Muon extension into LoFT-Muon with a factorized Newton-Schulz procedure (Appendix D.1). It also introduces LoFT (simple), which omits second-moment calibration. These are substantive procedural additions; the original LoFT-AdamW algorithm is retained.

E1.justification: v2 adds CIFAR-100 image classification and Python code generation, using CodeFeedback for training and HumanEval/HumanEval+ for evaluation (Appendices E.1, G.3, and H). Earlier coverage, including Orca-Math and WikiText-2 experiments already present in v1's appendices, is retained.

E2.justification: LoRA-Pro is added to both retained GPT-2/WikiText-2 comparisons (v2 Tables 14–15 versus v1 Tables 10–11). v2 also evaluates VPT and Adapter, described as ViT-Adapter, on CIFAR-100 and Diabetic Retinopathy (Table 19), substantially broadening the evaluated comparator families.

E3.justification: New protocols include 70B-model fine-tuning with learning rate 0.005, coding rank sweeps through 256, and context lengths of 256 versus 512 tokens. Coding evaluation samples ten completions per problem at temperature 0.5 and reports pass@1/5/10. These extend the evaluation design; the existing main hyperparameter tables and benchmark protocols remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's synthetic and GPT-2 ablations, v2 tests component removal on LLaMA-7B and ViT-Base/CIFAR-100. It adds second-moment-specific accuracy and memory analysis, component-level latency measurements, and coding rank/context sensitivity studies (Tables 6–7, 10–13, and 20–21).

E5.justification: Both versions report the main vision results as mean and standard deviation over three runs. v2 adds no new seed reporting, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty estimates. The ten coding completions define the new pass@k evaluation protocol rather than uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Main Tables 2–3 and the previously reported comparator scores are retained, but substantial new results appear. Examples include 70B average accuracy of 90.66 at rank 16 and 88.93 at rank 1 (Table 17), and HumanEval pass@1 of 0.460 for LoFT (simple) versus 0.421 for LoRA at rank 8 (Table 20). New ablation, latency, and vision-comparison results further expand the evidence.

T1.justification: v2 replaces Eq. 8's intersection-projection interpretation with sequential projections and changes the full-fine-tuning recovery condition from r=min(m,n) to r=max(m,n). It also corrects algebra in the update equations and adds factorized Newton-Schulz mathematics and explicit optimizer-memory accounting. These revise central mathematical content, although the original matrix-factorization lemmas and proofs are retained.

C1.justification: The abstract, introductory contribution list, and conclusion retain the same headline claims: optimizer-state alignment, full-rank AdamW recovery, removal of scaling-factor tuning, and improved adaptation without additional inference cost. The added experiments and variants do not redefine these summary contributions.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands the accuracy–efficiency interpretation: second-moment calibration is identified as the main memory and latency bottleneck, with little average accuracy benefit in the tested simplified variant. It removes the blanket statement about no additional overhead and adds interpretations concerning diminishing returns from larger coding ranks and stability across context lengths.

D1.justification: v2 adds an implementation-repository link, detailed Muon/Newton-Schulz pseudocode, and settings for the new 70B and coding experiments. It clarifies that PEFT's alpha/r scaling explains alpha=r in the tables and that Algorithm 1's full gradient is notation rather than an implementation requirement. These materially extend reproducibility information.

R1.justification: Section 4 adds a focused comparison with concurrent AltLoRA, distinguishing shared alternating updates from LoFT's AdamW moment alignment and asserting transformation-invariance novelty. References supporting the new vision and coding experiments are also added; the broader related-work narrative remains intact.

P1.justification: The supplementary narrative is substantially reorganized: v1's combined experimental appendix becomes dedicated optimization/efficiency, language, vision, and coding appendices. v2 adds limitations and Muon sections and revises the contents and cross-references. Main-text language changes are comparatively limited.

P2.justification: v2 adds tables for ablations, simplified LoFT, latency, 70B scaling, vision baselines, and coding analyses, plus four algorithm displays. WikiText-2 tables and plots gain LoRA-Pro entries, Figure 1's projection labels change, and retained displays are relocated or resized within the conference layout.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially improves support for LoFT's mechanism and practical efficiency. Real-model ablations and Tables 10–13 address questions v1 left unresolved about component necessity and runtime cost, while demonstrating a cheaper variant with nearly unchanged average accuracy. Mathematical corrections and implementation information further strengthen the paper. The new Muon material has inconsistencies—Appendix A still calls it future work, and Algorithm 5 omits learning-rate multiplication of the update—but these do not outweigh the substantial improvements to the core AdamW evidence.
